USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the Osaka pause on new tariffs and resume substantive talks without new US concessions. Hold List 1–3 at current rates and keep Huawei on the Entity List while allowing only narrowly licensed, non-sensitive sales; press Beijing for a written enforcement mechanism, IP/tech-transfer language, and visible farm purchases as a confidence-builder rather than a substitute for structure. Do not roll back existing tariffs or delist Huawei until China puts enforceable legal changes back on the table.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high. Existing Section 301 coverage is ~$250B after the May 10 List 3 hike to 25%, and China raised retaliation on ~$60B of US goods (effective June 1), hitting a key export sector: US soybean shipments to China plunged ~74% by volume and Oct 2018–Mar 2019 imports from the US were 21.7m tons lower than a year earlier, forcing a $16B USDA aid package. The 10-year yield fell from 2.74% (Jan 22) to 2.06% (Jul 17), and the Fed’s July 5 Monetary Policy Report said trade-policy uncertainty was already weighing on investment. That is material farm-belt and investment drag, not an existential supply-chain or recession shock — Wall Street was at record highs after Osaka and Empire State manufacturing rebounded from -8.6 to +4.3 once the $300B consumer-tariff threat was paused. The May 5–10 breakdown (US accusation that China tried to renegotiate; Huawei Entity List May 16; rare-earth signal; China’s unreliable-entity list) showed Beijing will not simply fold, so this is not a clean US opportunity either. Action should stay at hold/negotiate: Lighthizer/Mnuchin only restarted with Liu He on July 9; Reuters/Al Jazeera reporting through July 9 said China made no firm ag-purchase pledge, Huawei relief was being walked back to lower-tech licenses, and the two sides remain far apart on legal changes and enforcement — the same issues that collapsed the spring text. Escalating now would break a three-week-old truce and invite further ag/rare-earth retaliation just as China’s Q2 GDP printed 6.2% (27-year low) and US goods exports to China were already down ~30%. Conceding (tariff rollback or Huawei delist) would give away the remaining leverage after the May walk-back, with no matching offer on the table.
key_factors: Osaka truce: no new tariffs, talks restarted, existing $250B US / retaliatory Chinese tariffs remain
May collapse still unresolved: enforcement, IP/tech transfer, legal changes
Huawei still on Entity List; any sales relief is narrow and contested
US farm-belt exposure and $16B aid after soybean export collapse
China Q2 growth 6.2% (27-year low) vs US costs concentrated in ag/investment, not a broad recession
July 9 Lighthizer-Mnuchin-Liu He call restarted talks with no new commitments

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List.
G20 Osaka: Trump and Xi agree to resume talks. Existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs for the time being.
US 10-year yield 2.06% on 2019-07-17, down 0.68pp (~25%) from late January.
Sources say China did not make firm agricultural purchase commitments at Osaka; sides remain far apart on IP, subsidies, and enforcement.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin spoke with Liu He on July 9 to continue negotiations; both sides will continue talks as appropriate.
Oct 2018–Mar 2019 China imported 21.7 million tons less US soy than a year earlier; US soybean exports to China plunged 74% by volume.
Trade policy developments appear to have lowered trade flows; uncertainty surrounding trade policy may be weighing on investment.
China Q2 GDP growth 6.2%, weakest in at least 27 years; US imports from China-related trade pressure and weaker domestic demand.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Resume talks on the Osaka terms—equality, mutual respect, and no new U.S. tariffs—without making large farm-purchase or legal-change concessions until Washington puts a concrete path on existing 25% duties and Huawei licensing. Keep current retaliatory tariffs in place as leverage, leave the unreliable-entity list and rare-earth tools unused for now, and treat any soybean/pork buys as small, reversible goodwill rather than a down payment. The aim is to lock in the ceasefire, test whether Commerce actually licenses non-sensitive Huawei sales, and avoid giving Trump a free political win that he can pocket before hiking again.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. List 3 is now 25% on ~$200B (on top of the earlier $50B), Huawei and affiliates remain on the Entity List after the May 16 designation, Google and U.S. chip suppliers cut off access, and Meng Wanzhou is still held—together a direct hit to export champions and Made-in-China-2025/5G goals (timeline 2019-05-10, 2019-05-16, 2019-05-20). Q2 GDP slowed to 6.2%, the weakest since quarterly records began in 1992, with June exports −1.3% and imports −7.3%; Trump immediately framed that as proof tariffs work and hinted “possibly much more” (NYT/Guardian 2019-07-14/15). That sits near the CHN +0.5 anchor (major export/tech targeting) but below it: growth is still inside the 6–6.5% target, June industrial production (+6.3%) and retail sales (+9.8%) firmed, and Osaka paused the threatened ~$300B List 4 while talks restarted (timeline 2019-06-29; Al Jazeera/SCIO mid-July). Action should be mild because further escalation (activating the May 31 unreliable list or rare-earth curbs) would likely invite the very $300B hike and a harder Huawei cutoff that the slowing economy cannot absorb; maximal concession is also wrong—Beijing already saw in May that walking back legal/enforcement text produced a tariff hike, and as of mid-July China has denied any firm Osaka farm pledge while Lighthizer/Mnuchin–Liu He phone talks have not narrowed the May gap on sovereignty, subsidies, or enforcement (Reuters/Al Jazeera 2019-07-09; CNN 2019-07-11). Commerce still treats Huawei as blacklisted with a presumption of denial; any relief is temporary, non-5G, and expires/unclear after the Aug. 19 TGL (Reuters 2019-07-09; Ross/Kudlow). Negotiate, do not pre-pay.
key_factors: Existing 25% U.S. tariffs remain on ~$250B of Chinese goods; List 4 (~$300B) only paused, not cancelled
Huawei still on the Entity List; Google/chip cutoff and Meng detention continue; Osaka 'relief' is limited, non-5G licensing at best
Q2 GDP 6.2% (27-year low) and weak June trade, but IP/retail firmer and official target still intact
Talks restarted (Osaka + July 9 Liu He call) with a large gap on legal changes, enforcement, and tariff removal
Premature farm purchases or law-change concessions would surrender leverage after the May collapse; further non-tariff retaliation would risk re-escalation

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi.
China announces it will establish an "unreliable entity list" targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.
G20 Osaka: Trump and Xi agree to resume talks. Existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs "for the time being." Trump says he will ease some Huawei restrictions (Huawei remains on the Entity List).

Chinese officials said the economy grew 6.2 percent between April and June... the slowest pace in China since the beginning of modern quarterly record-keeping in 1992. Exports dipped 1.3 percent in June... imports fell 7.3 percent.
Trump said tariffs are having a major effect... 'with possibly much more to come.' Industrial production growth accelerated to 6.3%; retail sales growth jumped to 9.8%.
Huawei would remain on the Entity List... Commerce will issue licenses where there is no threat to U.S. national security. Temporary general license expires on Aug. 19.

Little sign differences have narrowed. Chinese side did not make firm commitments to immediately purchase agricultural commodities; any deal including purchases is dependent on removal of U.S. tariffs.
Trump complained China has not been buying the agricultural products they said they would. Chinese side said they made no firm commitments; Lighthizer and Mnuchin spoke with Liu He.
